analysis.one_liner: Bans junk food sales in schools by updating the definition of food of minimal nutritional value.
analysis.headline: Despite 32 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to a House subcommittee in May 2006 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1979, federal rules have banned the sale of 'food of minimal nutritional value' where school meals are served, but the definition was written decades ago and the rules only applied during meal times. This bill would have required the Agriculture Department to update that definition using current nutrition science — accounting for saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, added sugars, and calories — and apply it to all food sold anywhere on school campuses at any time of day, from vending machines to snack bars and school stores. The aim was to keep unhealthy snacks from competing with federally funded school meals and to address rising childhood obesity.
analysis.who_benefits: Schoolchildren and their parents. The bill targeted the junk food that students buy outside the lunch line — in vending machines, snack lines, school stores, and snack bars — which its findings linked to childhood obesity, weight gain, and rising type 2 diabetes. It would also have protected the federal investment in school lunch and breakfast programs by making sure subsidized healthy meals weren't undercut by candy and soda sold down the hall [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to revise the definition of 'food of minimal nutritional value' using current nutrition science, considering calories, portion size, saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, added sugars, and the link between diet and obesity or chronic illness [S2][S3].

Applies the revised definition — and the sales ban — to all food sold outside the school meal programs, anywhere on the school campus, at any time during the school day, closing loopholes for vending machines, à la carte lines, school stores, and snack bars [S2][S3].

Cites findings that childhood obesity doubled among children and tripled among adolescents since 1980, that only 2% of children eat a diet consistent with federal recommendations, and that obesity costs the country $117 billion a year [S3].
Allows limited exemptions for school-sponsored fundraisers, as long as they are school-approved and infrequent [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beverage and snack companies that sell through school vending machines, snack bars, school stores, and à la carte lines would lose a substantial sales channel. School districts and school groups that rely on those sales for revenue — vending contracts, fundraiser proceeds, snack bar profits — would lose income, though the bill allowed limited exemptions for infrequent, school-approved fundraisers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Snack and beverage vendors in schools

drawbacks.text: Schools and school-affiliated groups would lose revenue from vending machine contracts, snack bars, and store sales that many districts use to fund activities; the bill tried to soften this with possible exemptions for infrequent school-approved fundraisers [S3].

The bill would hand the Agriculture Department broad discretion to define what is banned across every school campus nationwide, which critics of uniform federal school food rules argue overrides local school board and parent decisions about what is sold in their own schools [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: school vending and snack channels sell exactly the foods the bill's findings tie to childhood obesity and diabetes, and the old 1979-era definition allowed those sales to continue. The real cost falls on schools that have come to depend on junk food revenue, and on students' ability to buy snacks. On balance, the public-health benefit to children outweighs the lost sales revenue, which the bill's fundraiser exemption was designed to soften.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Education Reform Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on April 6, 2006, with 11 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S3][S5].
On May 24, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Education Reform, where it remained without further action through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill accumulated 32 cosponsors, 25 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but the House never considered it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Snack and beverage companies kept their school vending machine and snack bar sales channel, and schools kept the revenue from those sales. No student or parent gained anything, because the rules were never updated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Snack and beverage vendors in schools

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 32 cosponsors

for.name: 32 House cosponsors (25 Democrats, 7 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor Rep. Christopher Shays, a Republican

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Chair John Boehner)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in April 2006, referred it to the Education Reform Subcommittee in May, and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended

against.name: Soft drink and snack food companies
against.role: Vendors selling in school vending machines, snack bars, and à la carte lines
against.what_they_did: Sold the products the bill would have restricted; the industry publicly opposed stricter federal school food standards during this era

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 25 Democrats and 7 Republicans cosponsored — but no vote was ever recorded, so how the full House would have split is unknown; the committee that buried it was run by Republicans.

industries.note: These companies' school vending machines, snack bars, and school store sales were the direct target of the bill's campus-wide sales ban; they profited by selling high-sugar, high-fat snacks to students during the school day. The bill's death preserved that sales channel.

industries.industry: School districts and school fundraising groups
industries.note: Districts and school groups earn real money from vending contracts, snack bars, and school stores, and would have lost some of it; the bill offered limited exemptions for infrequent, school-approved fundraisers to blunt that loss.
Federally reimbursed school meal programs would no longer compete during the school day with junk food sold elsewhere on campus, supporting meal program participation and revenue.
